record.paper_title: Open Problems in α Particle Condensation
record.context_brief: Hoyle analogues with extra neutrons or tritons
record.original_question: Do Hoyle-analogue cluster-gas states exist in non-self-conjugate nuclei with A ≠ 4n, for example ¹³C made of three α clusters plus one valence neutron or ¹¹B made of two α clusters plus one triton, and how do the extra neutrons or tritons alter the condensate character?

evidence.quote: Besides the 4n nuclei, one can expect cluster-gas states composed of alpha clusters with extra neutrons (as well as deuterons and tritons etc.) around their cluster disintegrated thresholds in A 6= 4n nuclei, in which all clusters are in their respective 0S-orbits, similar to the Hoyle state with the (0Sα)3 configuration.

It is an intriguing subject to investigate whether or not Hoyle-analogue states exist in A 6= 4n nuclei, for example for the simplest cases, 13C (11B), composed of 3α’s and one valence neutron (2α’s and one t). The pertinent question is in which way the extra neutrons will influence the Hoyle state.
It is very intriguing to explore Hoyle-analogue states in A 6= 4n nuclei.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In the framework of nuclear cluster physics, the Hoyle state of $^{12}$C is the second $0^+$ state located near the $3\alpha$ disintegration threshold and is well described as a dilute gas-like configuration in which three $\alpha$ clusters all occupy the lowest $0S$ single-cluster orbit, i.e. a $(0S_\alpha)^3$ condensate-like configuration. Such cluster-gas configurations, in which all constituent clusters sit in their respective $0S$ orbits near the cluster-disintegration threshold, are known as $\alpha$-particle condensate (Hoyle-analogue) states and have been predicted for $4n$ self-conjugate nuclei.

Consider non-self-conjugate nuclei with mass number $A \neq 4n$, formed from $\alpha$ clusters together with one or more additional valence light particles (neutrons, deuterons, tritons, etc.). Two prototypical cases are:
(i) $^{13}$C, regarded as three $\alpha$ clusters plus one valence neutron;
(ii) $^{11}$B, regarded as two $\alpha$ clusters plus one triton.

Address the following:
(a) Determine whether near the corresponding cluster-disintegration thresholds there exist Hoyle-analogue $0^+$ (or appropriate low-spin) states in which all $\alpha$ clusters and the extra valence particle simultaneously occupy their lowest $0S$ single-particle/single-cluster orbits, in analogy with the $(0S_\alpha)^3$ structure of the Hoyle state.
(b) If such states exist, characterize quantitatively how the presence of the extra valence neutron(s) or triton(s) modifies the condensate character of the underlying $\alpha$-cluster gas: in particular, the spatial extension (rms radius), the occupation probability of the $0S_\alpha$ orbit, the binding/decay-width of the state, and the coupling/Pauli-blocking effects between the valence particle and the $\alpha$ clusters.
artifact.status_search_result: There has been substantial progress: systematic theoretical investigations (e.g. Phys. Rev. C 98, 024325 (2018)) and recent studies of $^{13}$C and $^{13}$N have identified candidate Hoyle-analogue states (such as a $1/2^-$ state in $^{13}$C) using $3\alpha + N$ cluster models and real-time evolution methods, and the "Hoyle family" survey discusses analogue states in non-self-conjugate light nuclei. However, definitive experimental confirmation and full characterization of how the extra neutron/triton alters the condensate character remain ongoing, so the problem is partially solved rather than fully resolved.
